title: Nitrogen Storage Vessel

introduction.definition: A liquid nitrogen storage vessel keeps nitrogen as a liquid at about −196 °C in a stainless inner vessel surrounded by a perlite-filled, high-vacuum annulus inside a carbon-steel outer vessel. A pressure-building coil keeps tank pressure, and an ambient-air vaporiser turns withdrawn liquid into gas for the plant; a final regulator sets supply pressure.
applications: Back-up and peak supply of nitrogen for plant inerting
Cryogenic cooling, food freezing and laboratories

temperature.title: From −196 °C liquid to ambient gas
temperature.description: Liquid nitrogen boils at −196 °C (77 K). The vacuum-perlite annulus keeps heat leak so low that daily boil-off is only a fraction of a percent of capacity. Withdrawn liquid warms in the finned ambient vaporiser (heat from the air; frost forms on the cold lower tubes) and leaves close to ambient temperature. 1 litre of liquid gives ≈ 0.69 Nm³ of gas, so a closed-in liquid line must always have a relief device (trapped liquid → very high pressure).

script.narration: This module introduces the Nitrogen Storage Vessel.
A liquid nitrogen storage vessel keeps nitrogen as a liquid at about −196 °C in a stainless inner vessel surrounded by a perlite-filled, high-vacuum annulus inside a carbon-steel outer vessel.
A pressure-building coil keeps tank pressure, and an ambient-air vaporiser turns withdrawn liquid into gas for the plant; a final regulator sets supply pressure.
Typical applications include back-up and peak supply of nitrogen for plant inerting; cryogenic cooling, food freezing and laboratories.

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Nitrogen Storage Vessel.
Read level and pressure.
Check frost on shell (vacuum) and vaporiser icing.
Test/replace relief valves.
Watch for high boil-off: pressure rises, venting. Common cause: vacuum loss.
Watch for cold gas downstream: frost on pipe, brittle failure risk. Common cause: over-drawn/iced vaporiser.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
